1.pericope_label: The tabernacle set up at Shiloh, and the land subdued before them

schools.summary: Gill traces the move. They came from Gilgal, where camp and tabernacle had stood since the passage over Jordan; but the land being in the main subdued, that station was too far off, so they moved further into the country and nearer Jerusalem, where in time the tabernacle was to be placed. Shiloh lay in Ephraim, Joshua's own tribe, about two leagues from Jerusalem; Jerome puts it ten miles from Shechem and reports that scarcely any ruins were to be seen in his day, only a demolished altar. Calvin reads the assembly as a summons out of lethargy: the people come forward with no proposal, and Joshua upbraids them with having been sluggish and remiss in entering on the inheritance God had bestowed. They are blamed, he observes, not for neglecting the lot but for not occupying the inheritance divinely offered; for as the distribution by lot was a sign of confidence, so each district that fell to each was a sure pledge of future possession, the Lord by no means deluding them. On the ark's new station he calls it a lodging rather than a home: a subjugated place was safe from external violence, but it was not left to the people to fix the seat where God should dwell, and they had to wait for the period so often named in the Law, accomplished when Mount Zion was set apart for the Temple.

Henry explains why a move was needed. The tabernacle had stood at the centre of the camp, but now that three of the four squadrons which surrounded it were broken up by the removal of those tribes to their possessions, it was time to remove it into a city — and for good and all, so that not one of its stakes must any more be removed nor any of its cords be broken. Three things recommended the place: it lay in the heart of the country, nearer the centre than Jerusalem, and convenient for all Israel to meet from every quarter; it lay in the lot of Joshua's own tribe, and the testimony of Israel and the thrones of judgment do well together; and some see an eye to the name itself, Shiloh being the title by which the Messiah was known in dying Jacob's prophecy, so that setting up the tabernacle there hinted that in that Shiloh all the ordinances of this worldly sanctuary should have their accomplishment in a greater and more perfect tabernacle.

Clarke calls it a considerable town about fifteen miles from Jerusalem, nearly in the centre of the land, to which both camp and ark were removed from Gilgal after a residence of seven years; it was most conveniently situated for access and for safety, the Canaanites being so subdued that there was no longer any general resistance to Israel's arms. Wesley adds the practical reasons — the convenience of Joshua, who being of Ephraim and seated there might consult God as often as he needed, and of all the tribes, who being about the centre could more easily resort to it.

Ellicott identifies it with Seilûn and explains the timing: Judah's inheritance had been settled at Gilgal, but the assignment of the central country to Ephraim and Manasseh brought the leaders of Israel into that district, and as soon as the position of Joshua's own tribe was fixed the tabernacle was set up there.

outliers.observation: The later ruin of Shiloh showed, Calvin adds, that no dignity can screen from God's vengeance those who corrupt His blessings.

themes: the whole congregation assembled together at Shiloh
set up the tabernacle of the congregation there
the land was subdued before them

2.pericope_label: How long are ye slack? Three men of each tribe sent to describe the land

schools.summary: Gill settles the number: three men for each of the seven tribes, twenty-one in all, though some think they were drawn from all the nine tribes and a half and were thirty-six, and Josephus seems to understand it so, save that he then makes only one from each tribe and ten in all — a great oversight in that historian. Calvin sees nothing more incongruous than to send twenty-one men through a hostile country and have them trace it through all its windings and turnings, leaving not a corner unexamined, calculating its length and breadth and allowing for its inequalities. Every person they met must readily have suspected who they were and on what errand; in short, no free return lay open to them except through a thousand deaths. They would not have encountered so much danger from blind impulse, nor would Joshua have exposed them to it, had they not known that all those nations, struck with terror from heaven, desired nothing so much as peace — for though they hated Israel, having been subdued by so many overthrows they did not dare move a finger, so that the surveyors proceeded in safety as through a peaceful territory, under the pretext of trading, or at least of being harmless strangers passing on their way.

Henry finds two reasons for the delay. They were well pleased with their present condition, liking to live in a body together, the more the merrier, and, like the Babel-builders, having no mind to be scattered abroad and break good company; the spoil of the cities they had taken served them to live plentifully for the present, and they banished the thoughts of time to come. And they were slothful and dilatory: they wished the thing done, perhaps, but had no spirit to stir in it, like the sluggard who hides his hand in his bosom and finds it a grief to bring it to his mouth again.

Clarke traces the backwardness further back. They had so long been supported by miracle, without exertions of their own, that they found it difficult to shake off that inactivity; when all the people went out to battle they went with a measure of confidence, expecting miraculous help and confiding in their numbers, but when each tribe found it must fight for itself, for its own establishment and the extension of its borders, it was discouraged, and chose a life of inglorious ease rather than an inheritance which would cost much labour to conquer. On the survey itself Clarke thinks the twenty-one were probably accompanied by a military guard, since without one they might easily have been cut off by straggling parties of Canaanites. Wesley explains why three and not one — for more exact observation of the measure and quality of the portions, and for greater assurance of their faithfulness in the account they gave.

Ellicott takes the situation as thoroughly true to nature: the conquest completed, the two leading divisions of the host took their shares and were satisfied, after which the weaker tribes were left to take care of themselves — they did not venture to select their own portions, and the others did not come forward to offer them anything. Keil is careful about what the slackness consisted in: they were slack not merely to conquer the land but to have it divided by lot and enter into possession. The description Joshua ordered was not a formal measurement, though surveying was well known in Egypt and regularly carried out after the inundations of the Nile, so that the Israelites might have learned it there — the Hebrew verb does not mean to measure.

positions.position: dangerous enough to need a military escort
so dangerous that only the terror of God on the nations can explain their safe return — no free way home lay open otherwise

themes: how long are ye slack to go to possess the land?
give out from among you three men for each tribe
they shall divide it into seven parts

5.pericope_label: The land described in a book and brought to Joshua, who casts lots at Shiloh

schools.summary: Gill notes that they went undisturbed by the inhabitants who remained, the fear of the Israelites being still upon them and the providence of God restraining them, so that they passed through the whole country and took their survey without molestation. Calvin makes that deliverance the point of the passage. Had they crept along by subterranean burrows they could scarcely have escaped innumerable dangers; yet now, taking notes of the cities and their sites, the fields, the varying features of the districts and all the coasts, and meeting no adverse occurrence, they return in safety — and who can doubt that their life had been kept safe among so many perils by a wonderful exertion of divine power? It is said emphatically that they returned to celebrate the grace of God, which is just equivalent to saying that they were brought back by the hand of God; and this made the people proceed more willingly to the casting of lots, for their minds would not yet have been well purged of fastidiousness had they not perceived in that journey a signal display of divine favour.

Clarke warns against reading the two fixed tribes as a description of the whole land. Joshua does not mean that Judah occupied the south and Ephraim and Manasseh the north of the promised land, which was not the fact; being now at Shiloh, well inside the territory of Ephraim and not far from that of Judah, he speaks of them in relation to the place where he stood. He gives Calmet's paraphrase of the charge to the deputies — go and examine the whole of the country which remains yet to be possessed, do not take into consideration the tribe of Judah, which is on the south, nor the tribe of Ephraim, which is on the north of where we now are, but carefully divide the remaining land into seven equal parts — and thinks it makes very good sense. The survey itself he thinks worth marking as a first: this is, as far as he can recollect, the first act of surveying on record, and these men differed widely from those who had searched the land in the time of Moses, who went only to discover the nature of the country and the state of its inhabitants, whereas these went to take an actual geographical survey in order to divide it; and we may suppose the country was exactly described in a book, that is, a map, pointing out the face of the country with descriptions of each part. Wesley explains what equal parts meant: the seven were of equal extent or worth, for no tribe was so great but that one of these parts would abundantly suffice it, and there was no reason why the portions should be greater or less according as the tribes were more or fewer, it being usual for one tribe to be more numerous in one age which was fewer in the next.

Keil states the arithmetic behind the number: only seven tribes had still to receive portions, since Levi was to receive none in the land at all, and Gad, Reuben and half Manasseh had theirs already beyond Jordan.

outliers.observation: Had the tribes increased more, Wesley adds, and not diminished their numbers by their sins, they might have sent forth colonies and taken any part of the land, even as far as Euphrates, to all which the Lord of the whole earth had given them a right. On the casting of the lot before the Lord he explains the phrase as meaning before the ark or tabernacle, that God might be witness and judge and author of the division, so that each should be contented with his lot and their several possessions be secured to them as things sacred.

themes: they described it by cities into seven parts in a book
Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the Lord
the priesthood of the Lord is their inheritance

11.pericope_label: The lot of Benjamin, between Judah and Joseph, and its borders

schools.summary: Gill notes that this was the first of the seven lots to come up, and a small one, whence the tribe is called little Benjamin; but the land was very pleasant and fruitful, and Josephus says the lot was strait because of the goodness of the soil, since it took in Jericho and Jerusalem. Calvin finds the tribe's honour in the order rather than the size. Its limits were narrowed in proportion to the fewness of its numbers, since it obtained only twenty-six cities, yet an honour was bestowed in the mere circumstance of its receiving its inheritance before more distinguished tribes; it was set between the children of Ephraim and Manasseh on the one side and Judah on the other; and it had the honour of including Jerusalem, though it afterwards granted the place to Judah for a royal residence. What he cannot explain is the sequel: it is strange that, having obtained so quiet a locality, they did not live on peaceful terms with their neighbours. But we possess the prophecy of Jacob, that Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at night dividing the spoil; so they must have been by nature of a covetous and turbulent disposition, or impelled by some necessity not now known to live upon plunder. Gill adds Jarchi's note on the reversal of direction in the border: where the same stretch is described in Judah's border the text says the border went up, the measure being taken there from east to west and here from west to east.

Henry sees providence in the placing. Benjamin was cast next to Joseph, his own and only brother, and little Benjamin, who needed the protection of great Joseph yet had a better protector, since the Lord shall cover him all the day long; and next to Judah on the other side, that the tribe might hereafter unite with Judah in adherence to the throne of David and the temple. One clause puzzles him: the western border is said to compass the corner of the sea southward, whereas no part of this tribe's lot came near the great sea. Bishop Patrick takes it that the border ran parallel to the great sea, though at a distance; Dr. Fuller suggests that, since the text says only the sea, a word which often signifies any lake or mere, the pool of Gibeon may be meant, which is elsewhere called the great waters of Gibeon and is compassed by this tribe's western border. Henry then runs through the cities, twenty-six being named. Jericho is put first, though dismantled and forbidden to be rebuilt as a city with gates and walls, because it might still be inhabited as a village. Gilgal, where Israel encamped when Saul was made king, became afterwards a very profane place. Bethel was in this tribe, though it seems to have been held by the house of Joseph, and there Jeroboam set up a calf. Gibeon was here, where the altar stood in the beginning of Solomon's time; and Gibeah, that infamous place where the Levite's concubine was abused; Mizpeh, and near it Samuel's Ebenezer; Anathoth, Jeremiah's city; and the northern part of Jerusalem. Paul was the honour of this tribe, Henry adds, though where his land lay we know not — he sought the better country.

Clarke identifies the side of Jebusi as the mountain of Zion near Jerusalem, Jebus having been the city's ancient name; Wesley glosses the end of the mountain as where the mountain ends and the valley begins.

Keil traces the lines more plainly: the northern boundary coincided with Ephraim's southern boundary as far as Lower Beth-horon, where it curved round and turned southwards, its goings out at Kirjath-baal, which is Kirjath-jearim; the southern coincided with the northern boundary of Judah; and the eastern was the Jordan.

themes: the lot of the tribe of the children of Benjamin came up
their border on the north side was from Jordan
the goings out thereof were at Kirjathbaal, which is Kirjathjearim

17.pericope_label: The cities of Benjamin: Jericho and Bethel, Gibeon and Mizpeh, Gibeah and Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill fixes Mizpeh about eight miles from Gibeah, near Ramathon, which Josephus places forty furlongs from Jerusalem, and notes at the end of the list that Zelah was the burying place of Saul and his family.

Clarke reads two boundary names for what they carry. En-shemesh means the fountain of the sun, which he takes as a proof of the idolatrous nature of the ancient inhabitants; and Geliloth, since the word signifies borders or limits, is probably not a proper name at all. On one city in the list he parts company with Keil, supposing Gaba the same as Gibeah of Saul, a place famous for having given birth to the first king of Israel and infamous for the shocking act towards the Levite's wife, which caused a war in which the tribe of Benjamin was nearly exterminated. On Mizpeh he records the assemblies held there: the people were accustomed to gather often in the presence of the Lord, as in the deliberation concerning the punishment to be inflicted on the men of Gibeah; Samuel assembled them there to exhort them to renounce their idolatry; there Saul was chosen king; and it was deemed a sacred place, for the book of Maccabees records that the Jews assembled there to seek God when their enemies were in possession of the temple. Wesley explains why Jericho can head a list of possessions at all: though the city was destroyed, the territory remained.

Keil divides the cities into two groups, the first of twelve lying in the eastern portion of the territory, and identifies them on the ground as far as he can. Jericho is the present Riha and Beth-hoglah is Ain Hajla; the name of Emek-keziz survives in the Wady el Kaziz, on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho; Zemaraim is probably the ruins of es Sumrah on the same road; Bethel is now Beitin; Avvim, whose name means ruins, is unknown; and Phara survives in the ruins of Fara, three hours north-east of Jerusalem and the same distance west of Jericho. Of Ophrah he says more, since it must be distinguished from the Ophrah of Gideon in Manasseh: in the time of Eusebius it was a village five Roman miles east of Bethel, and it is probably the same place as the Ephron or Ephrain which Abijah took from Jeroboam along with Jeshanah and Bethel, and the same again as the Ephraim to which Christ withdrew when He went into the desert. Geba he holds a different place from Gibeah altogether: it was given up to the Levites and lay near Ramah, is named as the northern boundary of the kingdom of Judah and was still inhabited after the captivity, and it is not, as he once supposed himself, the Moslem village of Jibia, but the small village of Jeba, lying half in ruins and keeping relics of antiquity, three-quarters of an hour north-east of er-Ram, upon a height from which there is an extensive prospect. On Mizpeh he recalls that there the war with Benjamin was decided upon, Samuel judged the people and chose Saul as king, and the Babylonian governor Gedaliah afterwards had his seat; the Onomasticon puts it near Kirjath-jearim, and Robinson is no doubt correct in identifying it with the present Neby Samvil, two hours north-west of Jerusalem, a place which stands like a watch-tower upon the highest point in the whole region, with a mosque, once a Latin church, believed alike by Jews, Christians and Mahometans to cover the tomb of the prophet Samuel.

debates.question: Is the Gaba of this list the same place as Gibeah of Saul?

positions.position: yes — the birthplace of the first king of Israel and the scene of the outrage on the Levite’s wife
no — Geba of Benjamin is a distinct town, given to the Levites, near Ramah, and identifiable with the village of Jeba

themes: the cities of the tribe of the children of Benjamin according to their families
Jebusi, which is Jerusalem, Gibeath, and Kirjath
